1:
Who the king is divides them along one axis, and every position on it is occupied. John Gill refuses the Jewish reading that makes him Hezekiah, allowing that king at most the place of a type, and takes the words of Christ himself, whose sceptre is a sceptre of righteousness. Adam Clarke leans the other way, that the prophecy has Hezekiah primarily in view; yet in their fullest sense, he grants, the words cannot be applied to any man, since God alone can do all that is promised. John Calvin says the prediction undoubtedly relates to Hezekiah, under whom the Church was reformed after a wicked predecessor had overturned government and religion together; but the prophet means to lead us farther, since the restoration only shadowed out there was fulfilled in Christ. John Wesley makes the king Hezekiah, a type of Christ and Christ typified by him. Charles Ellicott would render it the king, and calls him the true Anointed one of the future, though not without reference to Hezekiah as the partial embodiment of the idea, which the mention of princes worthy of their king only strengthens. Matthew Henry takes the passage as a description of a flourishing kingdom, readable as a directory to magistrates and subjects, a panegyric on a good reign, and a direction to look for the kingdom of Christ.

Two place the section in the architecture of the book. Ellicott marks the first eight verses off as standing to the preceding chapter exactly as the earlier picture of an ideal king stands to the anti-Assyrian prophecy before it.

Who the man of the second verse is divides them again. Gill takes him for the King Messiah just named, a hiding place from the wind of his Father's wrath, which he bore in his people's room. Ellicott observes that the word is used elsewhere for a mighty or great man and probably keeps that sense, so the nobles of Judah, who had been tyrannous and oppressive, should become a true aristocracy, beneficent and protecting. Wesley agrees that each of the princes is meant, a shelter from the rage of evil men to the people under his government. Calvin keeps the king himself in view: since many rulers by tyranny raise more troubles than they allay, the good king deserves this peculiar commendation, and what was said truly of Hezekiah may be said much more of Christ.

The images draw out the best local comment. Clarke praises the shadow of a great projecting rock as the most refreshing shade possible in a hot country, since it not only excludes the sun but has a natural coolness of its own. Ellicott sees the two great blessings of an Eastern landscape, streams that turn desert into oasis and a rock throwing its shadow against the noonday heat, and notices that the word for rock is the one applied to Assyria a few verses earlier, chosen to point the contrast.

The opened eyes are read as the lifting of an earlier sentence. Delitzsch says no physical miracle is predicted but a spiritual change, the judgment of hardening repealed and the defects of those not among the worst healed. Ellicott calls it another reversal of the judicial blindness with which the prophet's commission had begun. Calvin sets it against the dreadful threatening of an earlier chapter that God would blind them, so the blind are enlightened, the deaf hear and the stammerers speak. Wesley keeps it practical, that they will no longer shut their eyes and ears against the good counsels of a religious king. Clarke alone works on the text, proposing that a negative particle here be read as a pronoun instead, a confusion the Masoretes acknowledge in fifteen places and others reckon in more, since removing the negative restores the verb its usual sense.
4:
The healed faculties come before the moral reversal. John Gill takes the rash for men who never gave themselves time to consider what was proposed to them, and who will now sit down and consider coolly. Charles Ellicott makes the heart the intellect rather than the emotions, the rash those hurried and reckless, the stammerers those with no power to speak clearly of divine things. John Wesley says their haste in judging was an argument of ignorance, and that the tongue which spoke of divine things darkly was only partly mended in the good king's day and truly changed by Christ. Keil and Delitzsch state the principle governing the rest: a third fruit of the blessing is the naming and treating of every man according to his true character.

The reversal itself is a matter of names. Adam Clarke gives each a portrait: the vile person is the pampered, brainless fellow who eats to live and lives to eat, giving little and that with an evil eye; the liberal is the openhearted, princely man who writes on all his possessions that they are for himself and mankind; the churl is the avaricious man who starves amid his plenty. Ellicott would render the second word noble and the fourth gentle, matching them to the Greek and Latin words for a gentleman, and observes that this exactly reverses the picture at the opening of the prophet's work, where men called good evil and evil good. Gill hears the Hebrew play in the pair of names and applies it, that men ignorant of spiritual things shall not be made rulers in God's house.

John Calvin explains why misnaming happens at all. When public government is wicked, covetous men are in power and honoured, because people judge virtue by wealth, so a poor man is despised though truly upright; good government detects the pretences quickly, since where virtue is esteemed vices are exposed.

Whether the passage promises a change of men or a disclosure of them is where they part. Calvin insists on the future tense: the prophet does not inquire what wicked men are but declares they shall be revealed under the reign of Christ, the heavenly light arising to expose hidden wickedness. Ellicott says much the same, that in that better day men would learn to see one another as they are and not as they pretend. Wesley makes it plainest, that men shall no longer be miscalled, since everyone will discover what he is by his words and actions.

The proverb about the fool draws a classical parallel and a caution. Clarke calls it a proverbial saying which a Greek dramatist expressed in the very same words, that the fool speaks folly. Ellicott specifies the error the fool utters as heresy, hollow profession, or open scoffing, any of which comes out in practice as violence toward the poor. Calvin weighs rendering the word wicked or fool and keeps the term he used in the previous verse. Gill turns it doctrinal, that a man without understanding of gospel truths can only speak foolish things about the sufficiency of his own righteousness, and is an unfit guide.

The churl's instruments are the tile's small crux. Gill rejects the readings that make them his measures, which two rabbis adopted, or his servants, preferring the evil methods by which covetous shepherds fleece the flock. Calvin allows measures but thinks instrument the more extensive word, taking in every kind of device. Clarke takes them for machinations and designs, and judges that in the following clause a word has been lost and two others slightly altered, making the sentence very obscure; he would render it that the assertions of the poor are defeated in judgment. Ellicott adds that words so generic may still carry an implied reference to the men who had treated the prophet that way, making even him an offender for a word.
9:
The address to the women opens a new section, and whether it belongs here is asked at once. Charles Ellicott takes it for a distinct sermon against evils the prophet had denounced long before, which continued unabated in spite of the reformation; it stands here, he thinks, because it paints the harem influence that lay behind the counsels of the king and his ministers. John Calvin agrees the words appear unconnected with what precedes, which promised the restoring of the Church where this threatens a people reposing amid riches; yet he finds no absurdity in joining them, since the prophets commonly turn to hypocrites once grace is promised to believers.

Whether women are meant at all is the tile's first real question. John Gill reports that some take the men of the nation to be so called for their effeminacy, and that the Jewish expositors understand the cities of Judea, the ancient paraphrase rendering it provinces. Adam Clarke adopts that paraphrase and reads the address as made to provinces and cities, adding that from here to the fourteenth verse the desolation by the Chaldeans appears to be foretold. Matthew Henry keeps the women and sharpens the charge, that to feed their pride and luxury their husbands and fathers were tempted to starve the poor. John Wesley says only that they indulged in idleness.

The term set to the trouble is read in opposite directions. Gill gives the phrase as days above a year, and reports that some apply it to the interval before the troubles began and others to their continuance. Calvin is emphatic for length: it is no slight consolation when distress passes quickly, but when no end is held out, what is left but despair, and the threat is of new afflictions after the first year. Ellicott reads the same phrase the other way, that days to the year implies not the trouble's long continuance but its quick arrival, like our own saying about a year and a day. Wesley dates it to the Assyrian invasion, and Keil and Delitzsch print the whole sequence, from this summons to the outpouring of the Spirit, as one continuous passage.

Ellicott takes the failing vintage figuratively too: the words are commonly understood of a literal failure of the vine crop and so of the wine for rich men's banquets, but a truer insight into a poet-prophet's language would see the failure of every earthly joy.

The call to tremble is read as summons and as sentence. Gill allows either, an exhortation to repentance or a prediction that calamity will come on women now perfectly tranquil. Calvin defends the repetition, since men asleep are not easily roused, and observes that men are in more danger from prosperity than adversity, flattering themselves when matters go smoothly. Ellicott finds a parallel and a contrast in the words spoken to the daughters of Jerusalem on the way to the cross, and notes that the call includes stripping off costly finery for sackcloth.

Clarke observes that the word for sackcloth is necessary to the sense but has dropped out of our text, being preserved in the Greek and other versions, and that the verbs are infinitives to be taken imperatively. Ellicott makes the same observation about the implied word, and adds that the forms are masculine, so the call is not limited to the women.

On the last of these verses the disagreement is about a single word. Clarke reports that the Greek, Syriac and Latin read the verb as an imperative, and that twelve manuscripts and four versions read a word meaning field where our text has breasts. Gill keeps the received word and offers three senses: the teats of cattle dried by drought, the breasts of women that yield no milk in famine, or the fields themselves, the earth being compared to a woman whose fields are breasts that now yield nothing.
14:
The ruin is sketched rapidly and the commentators fill in the topography. Charles Ellicott admires the bold pencil and rapid strokes of the outline, and identifies the forts as those of Ophel, the fortified south-eastern slope of the temple mountain. Adam Clarke adds what made the place worth naming: Ophel rose higher than the rest of Zion at the eastern end, was strong by its situation, and had a wall of its own separating it from the city.

Which palace is meant divides them. John Gill notes that the Hebrew word is singular, so two rabbis take it for the king's palace, while the ancient paraphrase makes it the temple, left desolate as Christ afterwards foretold; he himself begins with the palaces of princes, forsaken because their owners must flee. John Calvin is interested not in the building but the levelling: nothing however splendid is exempt, since men are dazzled by their own splendour and soothed to sleep amid their wealth. John Wesley says the place is forsaken of God, the joy of wild asses being the desolate ground they delight in.

The limit set to the desolation is the real question, and the dispute is when the Spirit is poured out. Gill argues from the length of the ruin that Pentecost cannot be meant, since that fell before the destruction by the Romans while the Chaldean desolation had not lasted so long; the pouring forth must be still to come, bringing in the fulness of the Gentiles and the conversion of the Jews. Wesley takes the opposite view, that the word signifies to reveal and the promise was fully accomplished in the days of the Messiah. Ellicott keeps to the structure, that there was a fixed limit to the desolation, and that the prophet dwelt, as an earlier one had, on an outpouring which should sweep away the frivolities of a profligate luxury. Calvin explains why the promise had to be inserted: since God had determined to plant his Church among these people, some hope had to be left them lest they faint. Clarke adds that fifteen manuscripts and two editions read the following word with the article, making it an appellative, a fruitful field rather than the mountain of that name.

The blessing that follows is read at three ranges. Ellicott sees outward blessings, themselves symbols of something beyond, giving place to spiritual ones, so that over the whole country the judgment and righteousness that had been lacking find a home. Gill widens it as far as it will go, to desert parts of the world where the Scriptures had no place and now shall have an abiding one.

Calvin uses the verse against a misreading of Israel's hope: the true condition of the Church is that justice and judgment prevail, for men ought not to be like cattle seeking only plenty of food; it is plain from this that the Jews were not confined to transitory enjoyments with hope fixed on earthly blessings, as some fanatics imagine.

The last verse is taken as agriculture by one and as theology by another. Clarke reads the second noun as the culture of righteousness, so that righteousness cultivated by peace produces tranquillity of mind and permanent security; then he turns from the text to his reader, asking whether he has the principle and cultivates it, and telling him that if he does he has peace of conscience and a sure hope of everlasting life. Gill is satisfied with none of the possibilities: the peace cannot arise from works of righteousness done by men, since there is no justification by these; nor quite from the work of righteousness within them, their sanctification, though that comes nearer, being God's own work and following the pouring out of his Spirit. Keil and Delitzsch read the prophet as congratulating his hearers in the face of a double judgment.
18:
The promised peace is inward to one and outward to the other. John Calvin argues that since the righteousness in question has its seat in the hearts of men, its fruit must have the same seat, so the peace here is that of the apostle's saying that being justified by faith we have peace with God; having it we are no longer restless within, as when the gnawings of conscience make us feel the wrath of God. John Gill keeps to the outward, Jews and Gentiles dwelling in peace with one another, free from the outrages of the enemy when the spiritual reign of Christ comes.

What the hail falls on is the real dispute, and five answers are given. Charles Ellicott would render the clause but it shall hail, taking the storm for a sharp judgment preceding the blessedness; the forest, he says, stands in prophetic symbolism for the rulers of a kingdom, elsewhere those of Assyria and here probably those of Judah. Adam Clarke keeps Assyria and guesses the city to be Nineveh or Babylon, though he calls the verse very obscure. Ellicott knows that reading and rejects it, since the city that follows is clearly Jerusalem, which shall be brought low, its pride humbled to the ground, in order that it may afterwards be exalted.

The other three look further off. Gill makes the forest antichrist and the antichristian states, so called for their numbers and barrenness, and notes that a hailstorm sometimes falls by providence not on fields but on waste ground, as the plague fell on the Egyptians and not on Israel in Goshen. John Wesley reverses the earlier figure: as the blessing turns a wilderness into a fruitful field, so the judgment falls on those who were a fruitful field and are turned into a forest, the unbelieving Jews; and the city is Jerusalem, which the prophet foresaw would be the great enemy of the Messiah. Calvin declines to name anyone. The prophets constantly describe the reign of Christ under metaphors borrowed from an earthly kingdom, he says, because our ignorance could hardly take in the blessing otherwise, and the meaning is simply that the Lord will remove distresses from his people and make them fall elsewhere; by forest he understands desert places.

The closing benediction is read as agriculture and as ministry. Ellicott gives the picture its final touch: the whole land irrigated by calmly flowing streams, men casting their seed broadcast, oxen and asses drawing the plough over rich ground, the country under tillage from end to end instead of the meagre pasturage of an earlier chapter or the thorns of this one; a spiritual meaning, he adds, underlies the literal. Gill takes the spiritual meaning alone and addresses it to the ministers of the gospel in the latter day, the word compared to seed and the preachers to sowers, who will sow beside many waters, among great multitudes and with great success. Calvin measures the distance the promise covers: the same land was to be overspread with thorns and its cities levelled, and now the people are called blessed because God will give abundant produce, which the prophet illustrates by figures, that they shall sow in marshes and send out their cattle without fear of losing them.

Clarke ends where he often does, in travel and natural history. A traveller's account of rice-growing answers this verse exactly: the seed is sown upon standing water, and before sowing, while the ground is flooded, oxen and asses are driven over it mid-leg deep to tread it into readiness, the young plants being afterwards transplanted in the water. He adds from two other writers that rice is the food of two-thirds of mankind. Calvin notes that some take the phrase about the waters for a rich and fertile soil, but that the universal particle in it leads him elsewhere.
